title: Pondweed bubbles: how light changes photosynthesis speed
examples: How does light intensity affect photosynthesis?
Why does pondweed give off bubbles?

explain.say: Put a sprig of pondweed in a test tube of water next to a lamp, and tiny bubbles start rising from its stem. Those bubbles are mostly oxygen, made by photosynthesis. Let's count them and see what light does.

draw.text: Pondweed bubbles: how light changes photosynthesis speed

explain.say: Look at the left of the graph. In dim light, far from the lamp, only a few bubbles come off each minute. Light is the thing holding photosynthesis back. What do you predict if we move the lamp closer?

Now follow the line up. As the lamp comes closer and the light gets brighter, the bubbles come faster and faster. More light gives more energy to make glucose and oxygen. Can you see the line climbing?

See where it goes flat? Past a certain point, more light makes no difference. Something else is now in short supply, such as carbon dioxide or warmth. That is called a limiting factor. What could you add to the water to make it rise again?
So light speeds photosynthesis up, until another factor limits it. Great experimenting! Wow fact: greenhouse farmers in the Netherlands pump in extra carbon dioxide to grow bigger tomatoes.

faq.q: Why does pondweed give off bubbles?
faq.a: The bubbles are mostly oxygen made in photosynthesis. Under water, the gas escapes as bubbles you can count, which shows how fast photosynthesis is happening.

faq.q: Why does brighter light speed up photosynthesis?
faq.a: Light provides the energy for photosynthesis. Brighter light means more energy is absorbed by chlorophyll each second, so more glucose and oxygen are made.
A limiting factor is whatever is in shortest supply and so holds the rate back. For photosynthesis it can be light, carbon dioxide or temperature.
asks: Why does the graph go flat?

faq.q: How do you make the pondweed experiment fair?
faq.a: Keep the temperature and carbon dioxide the same, use the same piece of pondweed, give it time to adjust at each distance, and count bubbles for the same time each go.
asks: What do you keep the same?

faq.q: Why do greenhouses add carbon dioxide?
faq.a: In a bright, warm greenhouse, carbon dioxide is often the limiting factor. Adding more lets the plants photosynthesise faster and grow bigger crops.
asks: How do farmers speed up plant growth?

facts: Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature can each limit the rate of photosynthesis.
Light intensity falls with distance: doubling the distance from a small lamp gives about a quarter of the light.
